title: Justice Department has issued subpoenas for Nevada voter data, state’s elections chief says | CNN Politics
text:
Source: CNN

The Justice Department has issued several subpoenas to Nevada’s secretary of state seeking voter information, markinganothereffortby the Trump administration to insert the federal government more directly into the administration of elections.

The office of Nevada Secretary of State Francisco Aguilar, which oversees elections in the state, said Friday it received “seven voter-related DOJ subpoenas from the FBI over the last three months.”

Aguilar, a Democrat, slammed the DOJ’s move to seek the information, saying in a statement that the administration is overwhelming states ahead of the midterms.

“The federal administration is inundating election offices with investigations and questions ahead of the election, and making sweeping claims of election fraud to the public before any investigation is done,” Aguilar said. “We will continue standing up for Nevada voters and remain focused on running a safe, secure and transparent election this fall.”

It is unclear what information the Justice Department is seeking in the subpoenas. CNN has reached out to the DOJ and Aguilar’s office for more information.

The subpoenas follow a slew of baseless allegations of voter fraud from the Trump administration and subsequent crackdownefforts.

President Donald Trump still claims without evidence that the 2020 election, which he lost to Joe Biden, was rigged, and the DOJ earlier this yearsearched the elections office in Fulton County, Georgia, which has long been at the centerpiece of Trump’s claims.

The Department of Homeland Security this weekbegan a surgein its efforts to investigate voter fraud in nine states, including Nevada. The department previously pushed states toshare their voter rolls for auditand has vowed towithhold grant fundingfrom those that refuse to adopt a broad set of election reforms.

The administration on Thursday alsoasked the Supreme Courtto give the US Postal Service sweeping power towithhold delivery of mail ballots, setting up a showdown at the high court less than two months before the midterms.

Earlier this summer, DHS announced that an audit of public voter rolls had identified more than 250,000 registered noncitizens in four states, including 16,000 in Nevada.

But behind closed doors, the department acknowledged to the state’s top election officials that it had “confirmed” just 185 of them,according to internal records reviewed by CNN. Another 6,200 were labeled “higher confidence matches” — but still required further vetting.

CNN’s Jeremy Herb, Priscilla Alvarez, Tierney Sneed, Gabe Cohen, Hannah Rabinowitz and Fredreka Schouten contributed to this report.
